# stm-meteo


A bare-metal weather station for the STM32 NUCLEO-L476RG, written in C with no ST HAL and no CubeMX-generated code. It uses register-level I2C drivers with timeout protection and SysTick-based delays. The official Bosch BME280 API is ported through a thin platform layer, and the Cortex-M4 FPU is used to show live temperature, humidity and pressure on an SSD1306 OLED.

**Project goal:** learn bare-metal ARM development by writing drivers from the reference manual instead of relying on auto-generated code.

![STM32 Nucleo board with a BME280 sensor and an OLED display showing live temperature, humidity and pressure](/docs/stm-meteo.gif)


## Features
- Polling-based I2C driver with timeout protection
- SysTick-based delays
- SSD1306 0.96" OLED display driver
- Bosch's official BME280 driver, ported via a custom platform layer

## Hardware

| Component | Part | Notes |
|-----------|------|-------|
| MCU board | STM32 NUCLEO-L476RG @ 4MHz | On-board ST-LINK used for flashing/debug |
| Sensor    | BME280 breakout | I2C address `0x76` (7-bit) |
| Display   | SSD1306 OLED, 128x64, I2C | I2C address `0x3C` (7-bit) |
| Pull-ups  | On-board on modules | Bus shared by both devices |

**Bus configuration:** I2C1 at 100 kHz, 3.3 V logic.

## Wiring

| Signal | STM32L476 pin | Morpho header | BME280 | SSD1306 |
|--------|---------------|---------------|--------|---------|
| SCL    | PB6 (I2C1_SCL, AF4) | PB6 | SCL | SCL |
| SDA    | PB7 (I2C1_SDA, AF4) | PB7 | SDA | SDA |
| 3.3 V  | 3V3           | 3V3           | VCC/VIN | VCC |
| GND    | GND           | GND           | GND    | GND |


## Project structure

The directory structure is based on the automatically generated STM32CubeIDE project layout.

```text
stm-meteo
    ├── Inc/
    |   ├── cmsis/
    │   └── drivers/
    │       ├── bme280.h (Official Bosch API)
    │       ├── bme280_port.h 
    |       ├── bme280_defs.h 
    │       ├── i2c.h 
    │       ├── ssd1306.h
    │       └── timers.h 
    │      
    └── Src/
        ├── drivers/
        │   ├── bme280.c
        │   ├── bme280_port.c
        │   ├── i2c.c
        │   ├── ssd1306.c
        │   └── timers.c
        ├── main.c
        ├── syscalls.c
        └── sysmem.c
 ```


## Build and flash

**Requirements**
- STM32CubeIDE 2.2.0 (bundles `arm-none-eabi-gcc`)
- NUCLEO-L476RG connected via USB (on-board ST-LINK)

**Build**
1. Clone the repo: `git clone https://github.com/kacpersalega/stm-meteo.git`
2. In CubeIDE: *File → Import → Existing Projects into Workspace*, select the cloned folder.
3. Enable the FPU: *Project → Properties → C/C++ Build → Settings → MCU/MPU Settings*, set **Floating-point unit** to `FPv4-SP-D16` and **Floating-point ABI** to `Hardware implementation`.
4. On the same page, tick **Use float with printf from newlib-nano** (`-u _printf_float`), so `snprintf` can format floats.
5. Select the Debug configuration and click *Build*.

**Flash and run**
- Click *Run → Debug* (ST-LINK, SWD). The program starts after flashing.


## Code ownership and credits

**Written by me:** the I2C driver (`i2c.c/h`), SysTick timers (`timers.c/h`), SSD1306 driver (`ssd1306.c/h`), the BME280 port layer (`bme280_port.c/h`) and `main.c`. An LLM helped with the BME280 wrapper functions and the sensor initialization.

**Third-party and generated files:**

| File(s) | Origin | License |
|---------|--------|---------|
| `bme280.c`, `bme280.h`, `bme280_defs.h` | [Bosch Sensortec BME280 driver](https://github.com/boschsensortec/BME280_SensorAPI), unmodified | BSD-3-Clause |
| `Inc/cmsis/` | ARM CMSIS and ST device headers | See headers in each file |
| `syscalls.c`, `sysmem.c` | Generated by STM32CubeIDE (newlib stubs) | See file headers |

The project layout follows a CubeIDE-generated project, but no CubeMX-generated peripheral code is used. Only the TIMINGR value was computed with CubeMX

## What I've learned

- **Register-level I2C:** I configured I2C1 directly from the reference manual (RM0351): GPIO alternate function AF4 with open-drain outputs, then the I2C peripheral itself. The one value I didn't calculate by hand is `TIMINGR` for 100 kHz on the 4 MHz clock, which I took from CubeMX's timing calculator using a throwaway project.

- **Porting a platform-independent library:** The Bosch API only needs read, write and `delay_us` function pointers, so porting it meant implementing those three on top of my own I2C and SysTick drivers.
